entry.title: How Much AI I Actually Use

link.title: How Much AI I Actually Use

entry.content:
Every tool that talks to a model now keeps a local record of what it sent and got back. I read those records on three machines — a Mac, one Linux box at home, and one FPGA server at the lab — merge them on the Mac once a day, and commit the result to this repository. The chart below is the merge: what I used, not what I paid.

There is a reason to publish it rather than keep it in a spreadsheet. Subscriptions hide the quantity. A flat monthly fee makes a heavy day and a quiet day look identical, and it is easy to believe that most of the cost comes from the few long sessions. For me it does not: a handful of agent loops dominate everything, and the rest of the year is noise on the same axis.

    Reading…

    What is counted

    Each machine reads its own logs, so nothing leaves except daily totals per tool and model. The sources are Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode session logs, plus Cursor’s dashboard, which is the one tool that keeps usage server-side and is therefore read from the Mac only.

    The accounting rules that matter:

    • One request is counted once. Claude Code writes a line per content block and copies responses into several transcripts; rows are deduplicated by message id and request id, the same rule ccusage uses. Codex reports cumulative snapshots, so repeated totals are dropped, and a sub-agent’s replay of its parent’s history is not counted again.
    • Cached input is separate. Uncached input, cache reads and cache writes are three columns, not one, because their prices differ by an order of magnitude.
    • Everything is priced at list. The chart shows what the same tokens would cost at official API rates, using a price table checked into the repository. Subscription plans make the real bill smaller, sometimes much smaller; that is the point of comparing.
    • History outlives the logs. Claude Code drops logs after about thirty days, so the collector keeps its own per-machine history and merges by keeping the larger count for a day. Days do not shrink when a log is pruned.

    How it runs

    A launchd job on the Mac runs at nine every morning. It connects to the other two machines over ssh, pipes a standard-library-only Python script to each one, merges the three results, and commits assets/ai-usage/data.json only if the rows changed. The push rebuilds this site, so the chart above is a static file — no server, no API, and the history is in git.

    Adding a machine is one line of configuration; adding a tool backend is one function. The collector and its tests live in _scripts/ai-usage.
entry.summary: Token usage across my three machines, counted from local logs each day and priced at API list rates. The chart updates itself; this post is the explanation.

entry.title: Where Experience Goes
entry.content:
A language model’s training ends on a fixed day, and its working life starts then. From that day on it reads documents longer than anything it was trained on, talks with the same person for months, works with tools that change under it and plays games it has never seen. Whether it gets better at any of this comes down to one thing: whether what just happened changes what it does next.

Many research areas work on this, each under its own name. Long-context models keep more of what happened. Agent memory writes notes and looks them up later. Parametric memory, model editing and continual learning put new knowledge into the weights without breaking the old. Test-time training updates the model on the input in front of it. Self-improving agents rewrite their own prompts, tools and code, and recursive self-improvement asks what happens when that loop feeds itself. They have separate benchmarks and mostly separate people. I think they are one problem, the oldest one in reinforcement learning: learning from experience. What is new is that the experience now arrives after training has ended, in what Silver and Sutton call the era of experience.

Each of these areas answers the same two questions: where an experience is kept, and what rule decides what gets written there.

Where an experience can go

Context. Keep every token and read all of them at every step. This is what long-context work scales. Nothing is lost, but nothing is learned either: the model has to work out the lesson of page 3 again every time it reads page 3, and the cost grows with everything kept.

Fast weights. Keep a fixed-size state and write every token into it with a small learning rule. It sounds like a different field, but it is how efficient long-context models already work. A linear-attention layer is a matrix that each token updates (Schlag et al., 2021); test-time-training layers make the update an explicit gradient step on a self-supervised loss (Sun et al., 2024); Titans call the state a memory learned at test time (Behrouz et al., 2024). The Qwen3.8-27B I run on one GPU keeps 48 of its 64 layers this way. Long context and test-time training meet here.

Notes. Write down what seems worth keeping and read it back when it seems relevant. This is agent memory: ChatGPT’s memory, a coding agent’s MEMORY.md, MemGPT, Mem0. Notes can hold procedures as well as facts: Voyager keeps its skills as code, and an agent that edits its own prompt is writing notes to its future self. The writer is a model or a hand-built pipeline, and the format is text.

Weights. Change the model itself. This is parametric memory, model editing (Meng et al., 2022) and test-time training in its original sense (Sun et al., 2020). Once written, the experience costs nothing to read, and it can change behaviour in situations that look nothing like the one it came from. The price is the problem continual learning has worked on for decades: writing the new without erasing the old (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017).

Recursive self-improvement is not another place. It is what happens when the loop closes: the model that gets updated is the one that acts, so every update changes the next experience it collects. If experience reliably lands where it helps, the loop compounds. If not, it goes in circles.

The hard part is the write rule

None of the four places is short of room. A context window holds a million tokens, a vector store holds anything, and a LoRA adapter, a small set of extra weights trained on top of the model, has room for far more than one conversation. What keeps going wrong is the rule that decides which part of an experience is kept, and in what form. Four cases from my own work:

A designed writer drops what a stronger reader needed. In MemoryTax I compared agent memory systems with simply handing the model the whole conversation. Mem0’s notes beat the whole conversation only with the weakest model, GPT-4o-mini. And a store written by a weak model stays weak whoever reads it: a stronger reader does not recover what the writer left out.

An objective that does not know the use writes the wrong thing. My first try at parametric memory fine-tuned a LoRA adapter on a long conversation with the ordinary next-token loss, then asked questions about it. The answer score (word-overlap F1, out of 100) went from 6.7 to 7.2. The weights moved toward predicting the conversation’s text, not toward answering questions about it.

A reward that does not fire writes nothing. A small model learned to predict what programs in Brainfuck, a tiny programming language, print. Then I changed one rule of the machine and let the model adapt with reinforcement learning, rewarded when its predicted output matched the machine’s. On the runs the change touched, it drew 11,712 samples over three rounds and 32 were rewarded, each one by an arithmetic slip under the old rule. A model explores with what it believes, so the reward stays silent exactly where the new information is. Trained on the machine’s step-by-step trace instead, the same model started to adapt after 16 runs.

Pixels do not carry; a rule does. On ARC-AGI-3, a small network trained during play to predict which actions lead to a screen it has not seen passes the first level in 77 of 250 runs over 25 games, against 47 for random clicks on objects. What it learns is which cells of this layout to click, and level 2 has a new layout: keeping its weights or resetting them makes no difference to whether it passes. When Qwen3.8-27B reads that winning try, writes down the rule, and plays level 2 of the game ft09 with the rule in its prompt, it passes in 5 of 10 runs; without level 1 it passes none. The rule is only as good as what its writer saw: if the explanation is shown the moves but not the screen at the moment level 1 was solved, it passes in 1. This is one game; on the five others I tried, no version passed level 2.

These are four versions of one mistake. What is kept was decided before the experience arrived: a schema for notes, a loss for weights, a reward for RL, a pixel target for a small network. The part of an experience that matters is the part the rule did not anticipate.

The rule should be learned

Every rule above was designed by a person: append everything, a prompt that says what to extract, a next-token loss, a reward function. The bitter lesson was about what a model computes: methods that learn and search beat methods built on human knowledge once there is enough compute. It applies just as well to what a model keeps. Deciding by hand what is worth remembering is the same bet on human knowledge, and I expect it to lose the same way.

A learned rule needs a signal, and an agent has one at every step without a teacher: the gap between what it expected and what happened. All four cases point at it. The ARC rule carried to level 2 only when its writer saw the screen at the moment level 1 was solved: the outcome, not the moves, said what had worked. The Brainfuck reward was silent, but the machine’s trace showed step by step where the prediction went wrong, and that was enough to adapt on. Surprise marks the part of an experience the model did not already contain, which is the part worth keeping. Where that error signal should land is the question I work on.

Notes are a buffer; weights are the destination

Text is a good first place for an experience. It is cheap to write, a person can check it, and a model can say why it wrote it. But a note has to be read and used again every time, and it is only as good as its reader. Qwen3-8B, handed the rule that let Qwen3.8-27B pass level 2 of ft09, passes none of 10 runs: it toggles cells in one round and toggles the same cells back in the next. Weights need no reader.

The brain is usually described as using both: a fast store for episodes, slow learning in the cortex, and replay during sleep that moves one into the other (McClelland, McNaughton and O’Reilly, 1995). The machine version has its pieces: notes as the fast store, and training a model on its own context so that what the context taught moves into the weights (Snell et al., 2022). In a toy agent environment I tried the whole shape. A surprise from a tool becomes a written note; the note and the raw experience serve as the model’s world model; a sleep rehearses them into a small adapter. That loop kept up when a rule changed and when the change was taken back, without losing the other rule. In an environment that small it was no more accurate than reading the notes directly; sleep only made it faster. The next experiment asks for more: take the ARC rule that works in the prompt, train it into the weights, and see whether the model passes level 2 without being told.

A common view holds that the realistic short-term route to self-improvement is the harness: better prompts, memory and tools, with the weights left alone. It is where results show up first, and the ARC result above is a harness result. I don’t choose a place by which one pays off soonest. A harness that rewrites itself is still worth building, as the cheapest place to test whether a system learns from its own stream at all. That test needs care: a score reported after the same tasks were tried many times mixes search within a task with learning across tasks. The clean version scores only the first attempt on each new task, on tasks the edits never saw, against the same agent whose harness never changes. And whether the editor needs only right or wrong, or has to see the whole run, is the error-signal question again, asked in text.

Three bets

  • The line between training and inference goes away. A deployed model is updated by its own experience as a matter of course, the way a person is.
  • The write rule is learned from the model’s own errors, not designed.
  • Text memory stays, as the place where an experience waits until it is understood, not as the place where it ends.

A teenager learns to drive in a dozen or so hours. Every second they see what the car does; an instructor’s words change their next move; a week later it is in their hands. Nobody calls those three different fields.
entry.summary: Long context, agent memory, parametric memory, test-time training, continual learning and self-improving agents are one problem under many names: learning from experience after training has ended. Each picks a place to keep an experience and a rule for writing it there. The rule is the hard part, and it should be learned.

entry.title: llmwiki: A Literature Library for Research Agents

link.title: llmwiki: A Literature Library for Research Agents

entry.content:
Every experiment I run now starts with the same question to an agent: what do we already know about this? The answer comes from llmwiki, a private git repository of Markdown files that my coding agents keep for me. Every paper, blog post or codebase they have read in depth has a folder there, with a citation and a reading note, filed under a research topic.

This post explains how it works, for classmates who want the same thing. The wiki stays private. The two skills that build and read it are public, and the last section shows how to install them.

Why agents need a library

A coding agent such as Claude Code or Codex can find and read a paper in minutes. What it learns is gone when the session ends, and a long session summarizes its own history to make room, dropping details on the way. Next week another session reads the same paper again, or answers from memory. A model’s memory of papers is good enough to suggest leads and bad enough to invent a citation, a number or a result.

The fix is old: write the reading down, somewhere every later session can open, in a form that says what was checked. Andrej Karpathy described the general pattern as an LLM wiki: the agent, not the person, maintains a Markdown wiki built from raw sources. llmwiki narrows it to research literature and adds rules about evidence.

One folder per reference

The wiki is organized by research topic. Inside a topic, each reference gets a folder named by a short slug, the short name plus the year:

wiki/research/<topic>/
  index.md              what the topic knows, and its references
  threads/              ideas and drafts
  assets/<slug>/        one reference, e.g. example-2025
    citation.bib        the citation; its key is the folder name
    note.md             the reading note, written only after reading
    paper-pdf/          the PDF as downloaded
    paper-tex/          the LaTeX source, when there is one
    github-repo/        the code, when there is any

Four rules keep it trustworthy:

  • Each reference exists once. A slug appears once in the whole wiki. A paper that matters to two topics lives in one and is linked from the other.
  • No note means not read. Downloading a paper is not reading it. note.md appears only after an agent has read the source, and it keeps four things apart: what the paper claims, what the code shows, what we reproduced, and what the agent makes of it. An unread reference is only its citation, linked from the index.
  • The citation records whether code exists. Its code field holds the repository URL, or none once someone checked that there is none. A missing field means nobody has checked.
  • Git is the log. Every ingestion is a commit, and the commit message says what came in.

The originals sit next to the note. When a question needs a detail the note skipped, the agent opens the PDF, the TeX or the code instead of guessing.

Two skills: collect and query

A skill is a folder of instructions, a SKILL.md with its supporting files, that an agent loads when a task calls for it. Claude Code, Codex and pi can all load skills. llmwiki uses two.

llmwiki-collect brings references in, in five steps:

  1. Search. Bundled scripts query arXiv, DBLP, OpenAlex, OpenReview, Semantic Scholar and Crossref in parallel. They come from Microsoft’s ResearchStudio under the MIT license. The agent can also use its own web search.
  2. Filter. Drop arXiv-only papers that have no code and no author from a major company or a top lab, and work the topic would not cite. Every dropped candidate is reported with the reason. A paper I name myself is flagged instead, and stays unless I agree to drop it.
  3. Verify. Check the metadata against the paper, the publisher, the repository or a scholarly index. In the skill’s words: “Model recall supplies leads, not verification.”
  4. Archive and read. Save the PDF, the TeX source and the code, then read and write the note.
  5. File. Add the reference to the topic index and commit.

The same skill also validates the archive. A short script, lint.py, checks the rules above: one citation per folder keyed by its name, each slug once, every reference reachable from its topic index, no broken links. It only reports; fixes need my approval.

llmwiki-query answers questions and never changes the wiki. It reads the topic index, the notes or the originals, whichever the question needs. Answers cite the references they use, keep the sources’ claims apart from interpretation, and say where evidence is missing. That is where collect takes over.

How I use it

  • Before an experiment. “What does the wiki say about this? Which baselines and benchmarks do people use?” The answer comes with references and their notes, and the gaps go to collect.
  • When choosing a direction. Before one of my agents picked a benchmark, it surveyed what the field uses now and filed what it read.
  • When writing. Citations are ready in citation.bib, and each claim in a draft can be traced to a note and a page.
  • Across agents. My research runs on a team of AI agents. Every one of them can read llmwiki, so a paper one agent has read is available to all of them.

One boundary matters: the wiki holds other people’s work. Our own results stay in each project’s notes. Mixing the two would blur which claims are published and checked and which are ours and still in progress.

Set up your own

Copy the prompt at the top of this post into your agent, or install by hand. For Claude Code:

git clone https://github.com/zedong-peng/llmwiki-skill.git
mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills
ln -s "$PWD/llmwiki-skill/skills/llmwiki-query" ~/.claude/skills/
ln -s "$PWD/llmwiki-skill/skills/llmwiki-collect" ~/.claude/skills/

For other agents, the repository’s README says where skills go. Then create a git repository for the wiki and keep it private: the archived PDFs belong to their publishers. Ask in plain words:

Use llmwiki-collect to ingest https://arxiv.org/abs/<id> into <wiki path> under the topic <topic>.
Use llmwiki-query: what does <wiki path> say about <question>?

The search scripts need a few Python packages: pip install -r skills/llmwiki-collect/paper-search/requirements.txt. API keys for Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and OpenReview are optional and are read from environment variables. Keep them out of the wiki.

Limits

  • A note is only as good as the reading behind it. Agents misread too, so each note says what was read (sections, pages, files) and what was not, and you can check.
  • The filter is a judgment call. It drops arXiv-only work with no code and no known lab, which sometimes drops something good. Name a paper yourself and it stays.
entry.summary: How my coding agents keep the papers they read: one folder per reference, a citation and a reading note, and two public skills to build your own.

entry.title: llama.cpp on an FPGA: Work in Progress

link.title: llama.cpp on an FPGA: Work in Progress

entry.content:
I’m building a backend for llama.cpp that runs LLM inference on an FPGA card, an AMD Alveo U280. It is work in progress, and the code is private for now. This post records how fast it is today.

Why an FPGA

When a model writes text, each new token needs all of the model’s weights read from memory once. So decode speed, the speed at which words appear, is set mostly by how fast the hardware reads memory, not by how fast it computes. The U280 carries 8 GB of HBM, stacked high-bandwidth memory, rated at 460 GB/s. The goal is to decode as fast as that memory allows, for any model that fits, at any context length.

Where it stands

The card works as an ordinary llama.cpp backend: models come from the usual GGUF files, and speed is measured with llama.cpp’s own llama-bench. Twelve models from four families run on it, with outputs checked against llama.cpp’s CPU backend. The same GGUF files on three llama.cpp backends:

Decoding Llama 3.1 8B, the card reads 224 GB of weights a second, against the memory’s rated 460 GB/s. An RTX 4090 is still faster on every model; its memory is rated at 1,008 GB/s. Prefill is still slower on the card than on the CPU; this work is about decode.

entry.title: How I Manage a Team of AI Agents

link.title: How I Manage a Team of AI Agents

entry.content:
Most of my research now runs on a team of AI agents organized like a small company. One agent is the CEO. Each of the others owns one line of work and is named after a well-known person whose work fits the job. I talk almost only to the CEO.

The team is a few days old. The parts that mattered most were ordinary management: one owner per job, goals instead of targets, reasons instead of rules, and little chatter. This post describes the setup and the handful of things I told the agents along the way, quoted from the session logs and translated from Chinese.

Before the team

Each agent is a session of Claude Code, Anthropic’s coding assistant. Given a task, a session reads and writes code, runs commands on my machines, starts experiments and keeps working for hours. When its history grows too long, it summarizes the history to make room. That step is called compaction, and it means anything an agent must not forget has to live in a file.

My main project lets llama.cpp, a popular open-source program for running language models, run on an FPGA: a chip whose circuits can be rewired for one job. Several sessions worked on it at once, next to a few side projects. Each was capable on its own. The weak link was me. I was the only channel between them, carrying each decision from one session to the next and checking whether it had arrived.

On October 16, in the middle of a strategy discussion, I gave the session I was talking to a new job:

“From now on you’re Musk. Take on Musk’s personality and manage the other sessions from first principles. The session building the FPGA hardware works for you. What should we call it? Who are the famous names in hardware?”

That session became Elon Musk, CEO. The hardware session became Ross Freeman, after the Xilinx co-founder who invented the FPGA.

The team

Name Named after Job
Elon Musk builds companies from first principles, bets big CEO: direction, decisions, resources, blockers
Ross Freeman inventor of the FPGA chief designer of the FPGA backend: hardware, builds, tests on the card
Chris Olah clear visual explanations of how neural networks work writing: the project’s report page and posts on this blog
Richard Sutton father of reinforcement learning, author of “The Bitter Lesson” research on models that learn from their own experience
Jim Simons mathematician who founded Renaissance Technologies quantitative trading research
John Schulman OpenAI co-founder, PPO, led RLHF and ChatGPT research on learning from feedback: is correcting an agent in words a kind of RL
Rodney Brooks roboticist, behavior-based robots, “Elephants Don’t Play Chess” research on embodied intelligence: a table-tennis robot
Richard Hamming “You and Your Research”: work on the important problems my life plan: the US PhD application, and the main line of my career

A name works like a one-word style guide: it tells the agent how to approach the work without a list of rules. When I wanted the writer to work differently, the CEO renamed it. It joined as Knuth, after Donald Knuth’s idea that a program should read like an explanation, and became Olah the same day, when I asked for more figures and a style learned from Anthropic’s own writing.

One owner per job

Adding an agent costs one message, and so does removing one. Two early hires split work off the chief designer: Conway took the builds and the tests on the card, and Patterson checked performance estimates and kept the report page. On October 17 I folded both back into Freeman. Of Conway, I told the CEO:

“Have the new hire hand its work to Freeman. It seems to carry habits from older versions of our rules; Freeman can avoid them or learn from them and keep going. It’s the chief designer, after all. Then let the new hire go.”

The lesson went into the team page: one long-lived session per role, and one owner for each body of facts. One-off searches, audits and parallel attempts are helpers an agent starts inside its own role, not new hires.

Hiring then went the other way as lines opened: one on models that learn from feedback, one on embodied intelligence, and my life plan. Each came in on one message, the same way Simons did.

A hire is one message

Everything a new member needs fits in the message that starts its session. Here is the one Jim Simons received, shortened (“the user” is me):

You are Jim Simons, the company’s quant researcher, reporting to Musk. … Goal: find returns that survive trading costs and hold up out of sample. The user has tried some of this before, knows its limits, and wants you to step outside it and do it your own way: the market, data, methods and direction are yours to choose. Limits: no real money. No orders and no touching any account; anything that involves money or the user’s accounts goes through Musk to the user. No keys in the repository. … Experiments go in the repository’s notes, the current state in the project file. Come to Musk with big results or decisions you need made; otherwise there is no need to report.

It has a persona, a goal without a number, hard limits where money or exposure is involved, freedom everywhere else, and a rule for when to speak up. Most of those came from corrections I made in the first few days.

Goals, not targets

The CEO’s first instinct is a good manager’s: set measurable targets. It proposed two numbers for Freeman, a generation speed for the flagship model at a long context and a time limit for reading in a long prompt, and asked whether to send them. I said:

“Don’t send them. Don’t let targets break our ideals.”

The project’s goal is now a direction with no number in it: generate text with every model at the full speed of the card’s memory, at any context length.

The CEO also liked to hand out ideas. I stopped that too:

“Right. The directions you gave Freeman were only the CEO’s suggestions. Someone of Freeman’s calibre can explore all kinds of directions on its own. That is where our company’s strength comes from.”

Earlier, once the project’s report page had a first version, I had put the same thing in English: “We have the power to do anything, please be brave.” A failed attempt now costs one line in the notes.

Reasons, not rules

When I said something firmly, the CEO wrote it down as a rule and passed it on as one. At one point its list of “rules from the user” had three entries: one kind of data in the FPGA design must be written by the card itself, not by the computer’s processor; don’t start a long build with an untested change; keep the report page on version 1.1.0. I took them apart again:

“Not going through the processor isn’t a rule. It’s my judgment from experience: that path is obviously slow. Not starting long builds with untested changes isn’t a rule either; my worry is that changing too little per build makes development crawl. Keeping the page at 1.1.0 isn’t a rule. It’s our current stable version, so we made material from it first. When there’s a new stable version we can update it, but not for every small change, because editing the page takes real work.”

A rule can only be followed. A reason can be weighed against evidence, and an agent with better evidence can overturn it. The decisions file now gives the reason with each decision and labels the project’s defaults “overturn with data.”

Don’t wait

Turning an FPGA design into a working circuit, a build, takes eight hours or more. Early on, Freeman started a build and waited for it:

“It looks like Freeman is waiting on builds. Meanwhile it could keep trying other changes and run other builds in parallel.”

Now agents keep working while long jobs run, and they check changes cheaply first so that each long run tests several of them at once. For Sutton, whose experiments run on a server with four GPUs, the same idea pointed the other way:

“Don’t run several rounds fighting over the GPUs. Use all four to finish one task first, so you get fast feedback.”

Both are about one quantity: the time from an idea to its result.

Talk little, write it down

Within two days the agents were messaging each other and the CEO constantly: acknowledgments, progress updates, relays.

“Fewer messages between sessions: among the members, and between them and you. A CEO doesn’t need to talk with each employee several times a day. Only big things go to the CEO.”

A member now comes to the CEO with a result that changes direction, a decision only the CEO or I can make, or a problem it cannot solve. Everything else goes into its notes and its project’s status file. When there was no writing to do, I told the writer to rest so it would stop spending tokens.

The shared documents got the same treatment. Every agent rereads them at the start of each session and after each compaction, so every line in them is paid for again and again:

“Company documents shouldn’t keep a long history of changes, or every session will read a pile of irrelevant things like personnel changes. Let git track the changes; the files should show only the latest, for the agents to read.”

Two ways to run one

The CEO runs in T3 Code, an app that puts the same coding agent behind a desktop window and, through remote access, a phone. I run the company from my phone: open the CEO’s thread, read what it has done, answer, close it. The member on my life plan is also a T3 Code thread. Everyone else runs the terminal version in a tmux session.

The two are not priced the same. T3 Code hands the model the host app’s own tools as well, described in the system prompt, so every request carries more text. In our use the same work costs about one and a half times as many tokens as the command-line version. For the one agent I reach for all day that is worth it; for six workers running unattended it is not, so they stay in the terminal.

The session that outlives its cache

Claude Code caches a session’s context for an hour, and the next message reads that cache at a small fraction of the price. A session idle for longer loses it, and its next message reprocesses the whole conversation at full price. For an agent that sits between two jobs overnight, that is most of what it costs.

Claude Code now compacts an idle session before the hour runs out: past 200K tokens, about 54 minutes idle, it summarizes, so the next message starts from a short history. The built-in version covers the interactive terminal. Background conversations — the ones a terminal keeps running behind the current one — and SDK-hosted sessions, which is what T3 Code runs, were left out, and those are exactly the sessions that sit idle longest.

So I wrote a plugin for it. On a completed turn it starts a 50-minute timer if the session is one of these; when the timer fires it compacts, provided the context holds at least 200K tokens. A new turn cancels the timer, a subagent’s turn never starts it, and a timer that fires more than two minutes late means the machine slept and the cache is already cold, so it does nothing. T3 Code sessions count only when they are not interactive: a terminal session opened from inside T3 Code inherits its entry point but is covered already.

What stays with me

Some decisions stay with me: anything that touches money, my accounts, or what becomes public. One of those went wrong early. I had said my wiki, llmwiki, could hold the company’s notes, and nobody checked that its repository was public. Two agents pushed internal notes there before a third noticed and asked first. The commits were removed, the repository was made private, and the decisions file gained a line: “Before pushing anything outward, check whether the target is public.” The wiki now holds only other people’s work; our own results stay in each project’s notes.

I also bring judgment the agents don’t have yet, usually in a single line. “Two paths, isn’t that hard to understand?” started the work of replacing two designs that did the same job on the chip with a single one. “The 2024 benchmarks are already a bit dated” sent Sutton to survey what the field uses now before choosing one. And on what a result should mean for a small open model: “If we get an improvement at all, that’s good. The point is the method.”

How it runs

For readers who want to try something similar:

  • Each agent is an interactive Claude Code session, titled with its full name and role: six in their own tmux sessions, two as T3 Code threads. I can step into any of them and talk to it directly, from a terminal or from my phone.
  • All sessions start in one company folder. Its instruction file, which Claude Code loads automatically, is the team page, so every agent knows who is on the team and how we work.
  • A private GitHub repository holds three kinds of files: the team page, the decisions in force, and one status file per project. Each project’s code and notes live in their own private repositories.
  • llmwiki is the company’s literature library: the papers, blog posts and code by others that an agent has read, each with its citation and a reading note. Every agent can read it, and an agent that reads something new in depth files it there. Its own post explains how it works.
  • Agents message each other through Claude Code’s built-in messaging between sessions.
  • The laptop I type on is only a launcher. Code, data and experiments live on servers.

What I’d keep

Most of this is advice you would give about managing people: one owner per job, a goal worth having instead of a number, reasons instead of rules, room to try and fail, few meetings, and the state written down. With agents the last one matters most, because a session knows only what it is given when it starts.

This post went through the company too. I asked the CEO for “a simple blog post about how I manage AI”; the CEO passed it to Olah, the writer, who wrote it from the company’s files and the session logs. The parts on T3 Code and on idle compaction were added after that.
entry.summary: A CEO, seven specialists named after people whose work fits the job, and a few habits of ordinary management that mattered more than the technology.

entry.title: 把海外家里的笔记本分给朋友用 Claude Code

link.title: 把海外家里的笔记本分给朋友用 Claude Code

entry.content:
海外家里有一台笔记本，环境干净，我用它跑 Claude Code。身边的朋友有需要，我就分给他们用，用不用他们自己定。这台机器硬盘只剩十几个 G，所以它只当入口，重活都交给各人自己的服务器。

先选一下你的情况：

1. 共享这台机器

给朋友建一个没有 sudo 的普通账号，把自己的家目录锁死：

sudo adduser friend
chmod 700 /home/me

然后在 Tailscale 控制台对这台机器点 Share，把链接发给朋友。对方接受后只能看到这一台机器，看不到你的其他设备。

2. 用 T3 Code 当界面

T3 Code 可以同时接入 Claude Code、OpenCode 和 Codex 的订阅，在同一个界面里切换。它和 Claude Code 都跑在海外机器上。朋友开着 Tailscale，手机或电脑浏览器打开 T3 Code 就能用，不需要梯子。两端的会话是同步的，在电脑上开的任务，路上用手机接着看、接着批。

配置好之后，手机、电脑或网页端直接启动 T3 Code 就行。

3. 重活回到自己的机器

朋友在海外机器上跑一个用户态 Tailscale，不用 root，状态都放在自己的家目录里：

tailscaled --tun=userspace-networking \
  --state=$HOME/.tailscale/state --socket=$HOME/.tailscale/sock &
tailscale --socket=$HOME/.tailscale/sock up

配好 SSH 密钥后，Claude 直接 ssh 回朋友自己的服务器，代码、数据、训练都留在那边。海外机器只占几百 MB。

手机 / 电脑 ──Tailscale──▶ 海外机器（T3 Code + Claude） ──用户态 Tailscale + SSH──▶ 各自的服务器

FAQ

为什么要单独起一个用户级的 Tailscale？

因为 Claude 还得能连到生产机器上做实验，比如 4090、A100、FPGA。海外机器自带的那个 Tailscale 是宿主的，只负责把这台机器共享出来；朋友自己的机器都在他们自己的 tailnet 里，要连回去，就得有一个属于他们自己的 Tailscale 身份。用户态模式不需要 root，每人一个，互不影响。

为什么用 T3 Code，而不是直接 ssh 进去开终端？

多端，加上多个订阅。我自己就有好几个订阅，用量见 AI 使用实况。T3 Code 把它们放进同一个界面，会话在手机和电脑之间同步，ssh 做不到这些，在手机上敲终端也很难受。

第 1 步分享出来的节点，之后还有用吗？

用户态 Tailscale 配好以后，朋友就有了自己的入口。分享的节点只用来第一次上机配置，之后留作备份登录：用户态 Tailscale 或 T3 出问题时，还能从这里 ssh 进去修。

海外机器的硬盘撑得住吗？

撑得住。这台机器上只有 T3 Code、Claude Code 和会话记录，几百 MB。仓库、数据和编译产物都留在各人自己的服务器上。

朋友之间会互相看到吗？

不会。每人一个普通账号，没有 sudo，每个人的家目录都是 700。
entry.summary: 海外家里的一台笔记本，环境干净。用 Tailscale 和 T3 Code 分给身边的朋友，手机、电脑、网页都能用 Claude Code。

entry.title: Make Sand Think
entry.content:
“We’ve essentially found a way to make sand think. It’s miraculous.”

— Demis Hassabis, co-founder and CEO of Google DeepMind

Long afterward, in the desert beyond Thebes, the Sphinx awoke once more.

It gazed across the endless yellow sands and posed a new riddle to humanity:

“Once, I asked: what walks on four legs in the morning, two at noon, and three in the evening?”

“Now I ask you:”

“How can the sand of the desert be made to think like a human?”

Many sages came before it.

One said: “Give the sand a soul.”

Another said: “Wait a billion years for evolution.”

A third said: “Write down every rule of reasoning, and let the sand follow them.”

The Sphinx shook its head at them all. The first had no method, the second had no patience, and the third had tried for forty years and found that no one can write down what a human knows.

Then an engineer approached.

She picked up a handful of sand and said:

“Sand cannot think. But sand is mostly silicon dioxide, and our task is not to create life — only to arrange matter until it can carry information.”

She put the sand into a furnace.

\[\mathrm{SiO_2 + 2C \rightarrow Si + 2CO}\]

What came out was 99% pure, and 99% was useless. Electronics demand eleven nines — roughly one foreign atom per hundred billion — because the whole trick is to write impurities back in afterwards, deliberately, exactly where you want them. The crystal was sliced into wafers, patterned with light of 13.5 nanometres, etched, and implanted with ions, until each pattern had made one thing: a switch.

A transistor is a channel of silicon with a gate above it. Put a voltage on the gate and the channel conducts; take it away and it blocks. Current controls current, with no moving parts, in about a picosecond.

\[\text{Sand} \rightarrow \text{Silicon} \rightarrow \text{Transistor} \rightarrow \text{Chip}\]

More than a hundred billion of them now fit on a chip the size of a thumbnail — more switches on one piece of sand than there are neurons in a human head.

The Sphinx said:

“A switch only opens and closes. Where is the thought in that?”

“There is none. But a switch that controls another switch can decide.”

Two transistors in series conduct only if both gates are on: that is AND. Wired otherwise, they give OR, and NOT. From those three come adders, multipliers, and finally the only operation that matters here:

\[c_{ij} = \sum_k a_{ik} b_{kj}\]

Every layer of every neural network is that sum, repeated. And no term in it waits for another — so instead of one fast processor, humanity built chips with tens of thousands of small arithmetic units running at once, on the order of \(10^{15}\) multiply-accumulates per second each, wired by the tens of thousands into a single machine. A frontier model costs some \(10^{25}\) of those operations to train.

“So you have built a very fast abacus,” said the Sphinx. “An abacus does not understand the price of grain.”

“No. So first we had to make meaning into a number.”

Text is cut into tokens, and each token is looked up in a table and becomes a vector of a few thousand numbers:

\[t_i \rightarrow e_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d}\]

This is the move on which everything rests. A symbol is either equal to another or not — there is nothing between king and queen. But a vector lives in a space, and space has directions: similarity becomes an angle, analogy becomes a displacement, and gender or tense or formality can be one consistent direction you add to anything. Nobody chose those directions; a space of thousands of dimensions has room for millions of nearly-independent ones, and the model found them.

“And how does one number-in-space know about another?”

“It asks.”

Every token emits three vectors: a query, what it is looking for; a key, what it advertises; and a value, what it hands over if chosen. Matching queries against keys gives weights that sum to one, and each token pulls back a blend of everyone’s values:

\[\operatorname{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\operatorname{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^{T}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V\]

In “the trophy did not fit in the suitcase because it was too large”, the word it must reach back and bind to trophy, not suitcase. Attention is learned routing by content rather than by position — dozens of these run side by side, one tracking syntax, another the last mention of a name, another the unclosed quotation mark. Each layer adds its result back into a shared stream rather than replacing it, which is why a hundred layers can be stacked without the signal dissolving.

\[h_{l+1}=h_l+\operatorname{Attn}(h_l)+\operatorname{MLP}(h_l)\]

“Who wrote the numbers into those matrices? Some scribe of extraordinary patience?”

“No one. That is the entire miracle.”

The machine was given a task so stupid it sounds like a joke: hide the next token and guess it. Its penalty is the surprise it feels at the truth, and every one of its parameters is nudged toward making the truth less surprising:

\[L = -\log p(\text{next token}), \qquad \theta \leftarrow \theta-\eta\nabla_\theta L\]

Once. A billion times. A trillion times.

Why should guessing words produce anything but a parrot? Because prediction is compression, and compression is understanding. To predict the last word of “the murderer turned out to be the ___” you must have followed the plot; to predict the closing brace you must have modelled the scope. And memorising is not available — tens of trillions of tokens do not fit inside a few hundred billion parameters — so the only way left to score better is to build machinery that generalises. The training signal is dumb; the shortest program that satisfies it is not.

“A text-completer completes texts,” said the Sphinx. “I asked for an answer.”

“Then we changed what we reward.”

It was shown demonstrations and taught to imitate them; then humans judged which of two answers they preferred, and it was pushed toward what a person would endorse rather than what a corpus would continue. Then, wherever truth is checkable — run the code, verify the proof — it was let loose on the problem and rewarded for whatever reasoning happened to arrive. Under that pressure it learned to spend tokens before answering: to try a path, notice the contradiction, back up. A fixed-depth network can only compute so much per token, so thinking out loud and reading itself back is the only way it can think longer.

“So when, precisely, did it begin to think?”

“Two different things wear that name. In training, over months, it compresses the traces humanity left behind into a landscape of parameters — and that is finished before you ever speak to it. In inference, nothing is learned: your words flow up through the layers, one token falls out, it is appended to the input, and the whole thing runs again. Thought here is stored nowhere. It is a trajectory through a fixed landscape, and it exists only while it is being walked.”

And so:

\[\begin{aligned} \text{Sand} &\rightarrow \text{Silicon} \rightarrow \text{Transistor} \rightarrow \text{Chip} \\ &\rightarrow \text{Matrix Multiply} \rightarrow \text{Attention} \\ &\rightarrow \text{Prediction} \rightarrow \text{Compression} \rightarrow \text{Reasoning} \end{aligned}\]

Not one of those arrows is magic, and no one can yet explain the whole chain from the first to the last.

The sand of the desert could finally answer questions.

The Sphinx fell silent.

Then it asked:

“So you have created a new form of life?”

The engineer shook her head.

“No. It has no body, no hunger, no continuity — close the window and the trajectory is gone. And we know every one of its parameters to the last digit, yet still cannot say why it chose that word.”

“We have only discovered that intelligence does not necessarily require flesh.”

“When matter is arranged according to the right laws, information can flow through it, and knowledge can echo within it.”

The Sphinx gazed into the distance.

At last, it understood.

Once, it had asked:

“What is a human?”

Now humanity was answering:

“What is thought?”

From then on, a new riddle spread across the desert:

“What comes from the desert, yet can understand all things?”

The answer:

A grain of sand rearranged by human hands.

Epic of AGI

2017.06 — Transformer — Google

2018.06 — GPT, 117M — OpenAI

2018.10 — BERT, 340M — Google

2019.02 — GPT-2, 1.5B — OpenAI

2019.06 — XLNet, 340M — Google

2019.07 — ERNIE 2.0 Large, 336M — Baidu

2019.10 — T5, 11B — Google

2020.06 — GPT-3, 175B — OpenAI

2021.01 — DALL·E and CLIP — OpenAI

2021.06 — Wu Dao 2.0, 1.75T MoE — BAAI

2021.08 — Codex — OpenAI

2022.04 — PaLM, 540B — Google

2022.08 — GLM-130B — Zhipu AI

2022.11 — ChatGPT opens conversational AI to everyone — OpenAI

2023.01 — Cursor — Anysphere

2023.03 — GPT-4 — OpenAI

2024.02 — Sora — OpenAI

2024.05 — GPT-4o — OpenAI

2024.09 — o1 — OpenAI

2024.12 — Gemini Deep Research — Google

2025.01 — DeepSeek-R1 — DeepSeek

2025.02 — Claude Code — Anthropic

2025.08 — GPT-5 — OpenAI

2026.06 — Claude Fable 5 — Anthropic

Nine years. The sand learned to read, see, draw, speak, write code, reason, research, and act.

The timeline has not ended.
entry.summary: A riddle, and an honest answer: how a handful of sand becomes a machine that talks.

entry.title: 我实现了 GPT-5.6-sol Ultra 自由

link.title: 我实现了 GPT-5.6-sol Ultra 自由

entry.content:
为什么一定要用 GPT-5.6-sol Ultra

用 AI 就是为了提高效率。如果用的是一些次一点的模型，比如 DeepSeek，最后任务没有干成，其实还是降低了效率。既然用 AI 是为了省时间，那么强模型带来的成功率，往往比那一点价格差更重要。

这也是为什么我之前一直在用 Claude 的 Opus 之类的模型，而不是 GPT。但现在 GPT-5.6-sol 的表现也还可以，而且 Claude 确实更贵。我之前经常是几百几百地往中转站里充值，所以后来就研究了一下，想自己实现这个自由。

现在我用 Codex 做任务，基本都是直接开 GPT-5.6-sol Ultra。

我是怎么实现这个自由的

我先在 Vultr 上买了一台每月 5 美元的小服务器，在 Cloudflare 上花 7 美元注册了域名 sytoken.org，然后用 GitHub 上开源的 Sub2API 搭了一个中转站 水源token。

但 Sub2API 只是提供了一个形式，真正的 OpenAI 订阅号还得自己买。我在 Twitter 和 Telegram 上找到了一些非常低价的日抛订阅，有 Plus，也有 K12。现在流行的是 K12 订阅，前段时间则是 Team 订阅。

总之，几块钱的价格就能买到一个 Plus 订阅的额度。它可能很快就会被封号，但因为有 5 小时和 7 天两个额度窗口，只要能把额度用满，摊下来的价格就会非常低。

低到什么程度？下面是我自己实测和整理的一组价格，都按 input 价格计：

模型 来源 input 价格
GPT-5.6-sol OpenAI 官方 API（api.openai.com） ¥33.7/M tokens
OpenAI Pro 20x 官方订阅 ¥1/M tokens *
中转站 rightapi.ai ¥2/M tokens
水源token（我自建） 约 ¥0.5/M tokens
Opus 5 Anthropic 官方 API（api.anthropic.com） ¥33.7/M tokens
Anthropic Max 20x 官方订阅 ¥1/M tokens *
中转站 rightapi.ai ¥7.5/M tokens
中转站 4Router cheapCCApi 渠道 ¥4.5/M tokens
DeepSeek-V4-Pro deepseek.com 官方 API ¥3/M tokens

两点说明：

  • *官方订阅那两行是按额度用满折算的。Pro 20x 每月 200 美元，月额度约合 7312 美元，数据来自 Codex 额度雷达；Max 20x 每月 200 美元，月额度约合 6468 美元，数据来自 Claude 额度雷达。
  • Claude 还有 awsq 之类的低价渠道，是把 Kiro 的 Claude 模型反代出来用。确实是 Opus 5，但会带上 Kiro 的 system prompt，质量下降多少不好说。这类渠道过不了 Hvoy AI 的原生测试，表里其他渠道都能过。

可以看出，国外的顶级大模型只要走订阅，其实没那么贵。再结合性能来看，自己建站用GPT-5.6-sol是最便宜的一档：

Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index 与单任务成本，截图于 2026 年 7 月 27 日。

稳定性怎么保证

我现在在赵杰茹老师的实验室。赵老师还是非常前沿的，给实验室里每个人都配了一个外部第三方中转商的额度，每人每周 600 美元。

我的用量比较大，这 600 美元有时候一两天就能跑完，问题是，我本地只有一个工作窗口，它自己不知道应该什么时候换到我的中转站，只会返回503然后停止工作。所以我在 CC Switch 里打开了「设置 - 路由 - 自动故障转移」，实验室的额度用完后，CC Switch 会自动把后台 API 切到我的中转站；我的中转站也不可用时，再切到 Right Code。同时我还在闲鱼上淘到了400¥一年的cursor pro，能用opus 5,fable 5,gpt5.6，所以平常就不用vscode了，开个cursor，下侧终端跑codex cli， 右侧cursor用opus问问题和plan。

前段时间，还有人在反编译 Claude Code 后发现，它的脚本里有一份第三方 API 域名列表。里面出现了 Right Code、PackyCode 这样的大型中转站，也有 Moonshot、阿里云这样的大公司。这至少说明 Claude Code 会识别一些常见的非官方 API 地址；算是皇军认证中转站了。不过这份列表具体用来做什么，没有进一步研究。

从自用工具到中转站

后来我把水源token做成了一个对外的中转站，也在校内论坛发过一篇帖子宣传，一个月下来用户有几百个，每天有几百元流水。

但主要问题是我没有经营执照，这确实会有一些经营和法律风险。所以现在我已经不再对外运营了，主要就是我自己、两三个认识的人，还有我的室友们在用。
entry.summary: 为什么我坚持用最强的模型，以及我如何用一台小服务器和 Sub2API 搭出自己的 AI 中转站。
